builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference
summary: FPoT replaces standard uniform-integer 4-bit weight quantization with a base-sqrt(2) power-of-two grid so that inference MACs become shift-add operations on a custom multiplier-free processing element. The cost is that the efficiency benefit exists only on dedicated hardware (FPGA/ASIC); on a conventional GPU the method yields no speed or memory advantage over mature INT4 PTQ toolchains, and it still requires calibration-time grid alignment and an approximate sqrt(2) adder whose error must be absorbed during weight calibration. It can fail through residual accuracy loss versus full precision in aggressive W4A4 settings, through approximation error from the 1-adder sqrt(2) unit if calibration does not fully compensate, and through the absence of deployable kernels for commodity accelerators.
rationale: The paper's gains are realized only in custom shift-add hardware, which is incompatible with the reader's 24 GB GPU or API-based setup, where established INT4 PTQ methods already deliver the practical benefit.

claims.statement: FPoT replaces standard uniform-integer 4-bit weight quantization with a base-sqrt(2) power-of-two grid so that inference MACs become shift-add operations on a custom multiplier-free processing element. The cost is that the efficiency benefit exists only on dedicated hardware (FPGA/ASIC); on a conventional GPU the method yields no speed or memory advantage over mature INT4 PTQ toolchains, and it still requires calibration-time grid alignment and an approximate sqrt(2) adder whose error must be absorbed during weight calibration. It can fail through residual accuracy loss versus full precision in aggressive W4A4 settings, through approximation error from the 1-adder sqrt(2) unit if calibration does not fully compensate, and through the absence of deployable kernels for commodity accelerators.

On Llama-3-8B with W4A4, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning by 8.72% over the PoT baseline and trails the uniform INT4 baseline by only 0.4 percentage points; validated across seven models and three bit-widths.
